main.title: Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island
main.summary: Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island is a 1995 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.heading: Yoshi carries Baby Mario
cards.text: Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island is a 1995 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). The player controls Yoshi dinosaurs on their quest to reunite baby Mario with his brother Luigi, who has been kidnapped by the wizard Kamek. Yoshi runs and jumps to reach the end of each level while solving puzzles and collecting items with Mario's help.

cards.heading: Hand-drawn artwork and Super FX2
cards.text: Having introduced the character in the previous Super Mario game, Super Mario World (1990), Nintendo decided to develop a game starring Yoshi, with the aim of making it more accessible. Yoshi's Island introduced his signature flutter jump and egg-spawning abilities. The marker-drawn art style was created by scanning hand-drawn pictures and approximating them pixel-by-pixel. Some special effects were powered by a new Super FX2 microchip.

cards.heading: Exploring worlds and finding collectibles
cards.text: Yoshi's Island is a 2D side-scrolling platform game. In the Super Mario series platform game tradition, the player controls Yoshi in run-and-jump gameplay. The player navigates between platforms and atop some foes en route to the end of the increasingly difficult levels. The player characters are Yoshis who take turns traveling through 48 levels across six worlds to rescue Baby Luigi and reunite the brothers. Yoshi also collects coins to earn extra lives and retains his long tongue from Super Mario World. The game centers more on "puzzle-solving and item-collecting" than other platformers, with hidden flowers and red coins to find. Levels include mines, ski jumps, and "the requisite fiery dungeons". Every fourth level (two in each world) is a boss fight against a large version of a previous foe.

cards.heading: Aiming eggs and transforming Yoshi
cards.text: The crayon-like scenery gives Yoshi's movement a playful setting, but his abilities make it practical. Holding jump produces a flutter that extends a crossing; a ground pound breaks soft earth or buries objects. His tongue catches enemies, which can be spat back immediately or stored as eggs. Aiming those eggs lets the player strike obstacles directly or bounce shots off surfaces, with up to six following behind. Temporary transformations turn Yoshi into vehicles such as a helicopter or submarine, changing how a section is explored.

cards.heading: Recovering Baby Mario before time runs out
cards.text: A hit sends Baby Mario floating away in a bubble while a timer counts down. The player must recover him before the Koopas arrive, turning damage into a short rescue rather than an immediate loss. Collecting stars replenishes that time, although pits, spikes and lava remain fatal. At each stage's end, one Yoshi passes Mario to the next. Flowers, red coins and a full timer also make completion a second challenge: perfect results across a world's eight stages unlock two hidden levels.

cards.heading: Release and reception
cards.text: After four years of development, Yoshi's Island was released in Japan in August 1995 and worldwide two months later. It sold more than four million copies. Critics described it as one of the greatest video games of all time, praising the art, sound, level design and gameplay. The art style and Yoshi's signature characteristics established the Yoshi series of spin-offs and sequels.

cards.heading: Later editions and rereleases
cards.text: Yoshi's Island was the last Super Mario platformer before the series' transition to 3D gameplay, with no further 2D entries for over a decade. It was ported to the Game Boy Advance as Yoshi's Island: Super Mario Advance 3 in 2002; this version was rereleased for the Nintendo 3DS and the Wii U's Virtual Console. The original version was also released for the Super NES Classic Edition, and both versions for the Nintendo Classics service.

main.title: Shining Wisdom
main.subtitle: A squire in Odegan
main.summary: Shining Wisdom is Sonic! Software Planning and Camelot's action adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 11 August 1995.

cards.heading: A squire in Odegan
cards.text: Shining Wisdom is Sonic! Software Planning and Camelot's action adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 11 August 1995. The player controls Mars, a young squire in Odegan who becomes involved in the dark elf Pazort's plans against the kingdom. The story follows a single adventurer through an overhead world of enemies and puzzles. Sword attacks and movement take place directly in that world, giving this Shining game a different rhythm from the party-based battles associated with much of the series. Progress comes through exploration and the useful equipment found along the way.

cards.heading: Equipment changes the journey
cards.text: Mars uses combinations of acquired items and magical orbs to expand what he can do. Choosing that equipment matters to both combat and obstacles, giving the player a reason to reconsider a route after finding something new. His attacks depend on direct control and movement rather than a party's turn-based commands. The large world places puzzles between its confrontations, so knowing where an ability can be applied becomes part of navigation. A new item can make an earlier obstruction into a useful destination, connecting collection with a concrete change in the journey.

cards.heading: A different branch of Shining
cards.text: The project began as a Mega Drive game before being adapted for Saturn, retaining a two-dimensional structure with pre-rendered character sprites. Its story also connects to Shining Force II through the setting of Parmecia and returning characters, although changes in the North American translation obscured those links. Motoaki Takenouchi composed the music. Shining Wisdom shows how broadly the series could interpret an adventure: the continuing fictional world remained, while the player's attention moved towards one character's speed, equipment and ability to solve a passage directly.

main.title: Magic Knight Rayearth
main.subtitle: Three girls in Cephiro
main.summary: Magic Knight Rayearth is Sega's action role-playing game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 25 August 1995.

cards.heading: Three girls in Cephiro
cards.text: Magic Knight Rayearth is Sega's action role-playing game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 25 August 1995. Based on CLAMP's manga and its animated adaptation, it draws Hikaru, Umi and Fuu from a school visit to Tokyo Tower into Cephiro. They must become the Magic Knights and rescue Princess Emeraude to find a way home. The adventure follows that first major story while adding locations and characters of its own. Rieko Kodama directed a game that presents the three heroines as companions sharing a single journey through an unfamiliar world.

cards.heading: One companion takes the lead
cards.text: The party travels together, but only one heroine is active in a fight. The other two follow safely behind, and the player can switch the lead at any time. That arrangement turns the group into a tag team for enemies, puzzles and environmental dangers, making the choice of the active character part of handling the next obstacle. The inactive companions remain present without requiring the player to protect three separate figures simultaneously. Changing who leads therefore provides a direct way to use the party's variety within the same continuous adventure.

cards.heading: An adventure seen through three journals
cards.text: Each girl keeps a journal that gains entries after important events. Reading them gives the player another perspective on experiences already shared, allowing the companions' individual reactions to sit alongside the main story. Working Designs brought the game to North America in December 1998 after a lengthy localisation, making it that region's final Saturn release. The long delay placed an early Japanese Saturn adventure at the other end of the console's American life. Its illustrated presentation and three-character viewpoint preserved a very different kind of journey from the machine's prominent arcade conversions.

main.title: Pulstar
main.subtitle: A careful route through alien space
main.summary: Pulstar is Aicom's horizontally scrolling shooter, released for Neo Geo arcades in Japan on 28 August 1995.

cards.heading: A careful route through alien space
cards.text: Pulstar is Aicom's horizontally scrolling shooter, released for Neo Geo arcades in Japan on 28 August 1995. The Dino246 spacecraft crosses eight stages to confront an alien threat to the Solar System. Enemy formations, projectiles and moving obstacles demand a carefully judged route, with a boss at the end of each stage. Its charged weapons and protective equipment give the player several tools, but survival depends on understanding how the next obstacle fits into the limited space around the ship.

cards.heading: Charge, shield or sacrifice the drone
cards.text: Holding the fire button builds a charge shown on a meter. One portion produces a powerful focused shot, while another enables a rapid barrage, allowing the player to prepare a response before an enemy arrives. An auxiliary drone blocks fire and can ram smaller opponents. Sacrificing it creates a powerful explosion, exchanging continuing protection for an immediate advantage. Power-ups add speed and supporting craft. The choices remain connected: using a defensive resource to clear a dangerous moment changes the equipment available for the passage that follows.

cards.heading: Rendered spectacle on Neo Geo
cards.text: Pulstar was the first Neo Geo game to incorporate three-dimensional pre-rendered visuals, producing detailed ships and environments within a two-dimensional shooter. Harumi Fujita and Yasuaki Fujita composed the music. The game reached AES that September and Neo Geo CD in October. Its severe challenge made learning routes particularly important, while its visual technique gave those routes a distinctive density. Yumekobo's later Blazing Star developed the approach with a broader choice of ships and a more forgiving balance, making Pulstar the demanding starting point of that short lineage.

main.title: Rayman
main.summary: Rayman is a 1995 platform game developed by Ubi Pictures and published by Ubi Soft.

cards.text: Rayman is a 1995 platform game developed by Ubi Pictures and published by Ubi Soft. The player controls Rayman, who must pursue Mr. Dark to recover the Great Protoon that used to keep the balance between nature and the people of Rayman's valley. The player must navigate the valley, defeat enemies with abilities gained throughout the game, and free captured Electoons, while also encountering a boss at the end of each thematic world.

Michel Ancel originally conceived Rayman as a teenager, and was later able to realise the concept after being hired by Ubi Soft in 1989. The game initially targeted the Atari ST, and then the Super NES CD-ROM, but development was moved to the Atari Jaguar after the peripheral's cancellation. Ancel incorporated several childhood memories into the design and was soon joined by a larger development team. Ubi Soft made Rayman a launch title for the PlayStation in North America and Europe to compete with Japanese platform games on the console.

Rayman was first released for the PlayStation on 7 September 1995, and shortly thereafter for the Atari Jaguar, Sega Saturn, and MS-DOS. The game received positive reviews, with praise going towards its atmosphere, visuals, and soundtrack, though some criticized its high difficulty and lack of originality. Rayman became one of the best-selling PlayStation games and would become the first entry in the Rayman series. A 30th Anniversary Edition for modern platforms featuring bonus content and a compilation of ports, including a prototype of the cancelled Super NES version, was released in February 2026 in partnership between Ubisoft and Digital Eclipse.

main.title: Tails Adventure
main.subtitle: Tails explores Cocoa Island
main.summary: Tails Adventure is Aspect's exploration platform game, first released for Game Gear in Japan on 22 September 1995.

cards.heading: Tails explores Cocoa Island
cards.text: Tails Adventure is Aspect's exploration platform game, first released for Game Gear in Japan on 22 September 1995. Tails sets out to protect Cocoa Island from the Kukku Army, gathering gadgets and abilities across its interconnected areas. Walking, limited flight and careful investigation give his solo adventure a different pace from Sonic's races. New equipment opens paths in previously visited stages, making the island a place to learn and revisit. The character's interest in machinery becomes central to how the player deals with enemies, narrow spaces and barriers along the route.

cards.heading: Four tools before setting out
cards.text: Tails can take four tools into a stage, with one equipped at a time. Bombs and hammers deal with enemies, while other devices support exploration. A small remote-controlled robot can scout ahead and enter gaps too narrow for Tails himself. Choosing the loadout therefore matters before setting out, since a missing tool may require leaving the stage and returning with another selection. Discovering a barrier provides useful information even when it cannot yet be crossed, giving the next trip a destination and a reason to change equipment.

cards.heading: A familiar place with a new opening
cards.text: Chaos Emeralds extend Tails' flight time, while rings act as health and are lost gradually when he is hurt. These improvements make the growing collection useful to survival as well as access. Twelve non-linear stages and twenty-six items give the island a substantial network of possibilities within the handheld format. Kojiro Mikusa composed the music. The appeal comes from the character's practical inventiveness: a newly found machine can change an earlier problem, allowing a place that seemed exhausted to become the start of another part of the adventure.

main.title: Command & Conquer
main.summary: Command & Conquer (also known by the retronym Command & Conquer: Tiberian Dawn) is a real-time strategy video game developed and published by Westwood Studios in 1995.

cards.heading: GDI and the Brotherhood of Nod
cards.text: Command & Conquer (also known by the retronym Command & Conquer: Tiberian Dawn) is a real-time strategy video game developed and published by Westwood Studios in 1995. Set in an alternate history, the game tells the story of a world war between two globalized factions: the Global Defense Initiative of the United Nations and a revolutionary militant organization called the Brotherhood of Nod, led by the mysterious Kane.

cards.heading: Modern Warfare and Full-Motion Video
cards.text: Westwood conceived Command & Conquer during the final stages of the development of Dune II, and it expands on ideas explored in that title. Inspired by the events of the era, particularly the Gulf War, the team gave the game a modern warfare setting. The game contains live-action full motion video cutscenes, which star Westwood employees and few professional actors, including Joseph D. Kucan, who plays Kane. The Nintendo 64 port was developed by Looking Glass Studios.

cards.heading: A Defining Real-Time Strategy Game
cards.text: Command & Conquer was a commercial and critical success, selling over three million copies and winning numerous awards. It has been cited as one of the greatest games ever made, and the title that defined and popularized the real-time strategy genre. The game was the first in the Command & Conquer series, which sold 30 million copies by 2009. To mark the 12th anniversary of the franchise, Electronic Arts, the current publisher and owner of the series, released the game for free in 2007.

cards.heading: The Remastered Collection
cards.text: A remastered version of the game was released in 2020 as part of the Command & Conquer Remastered Collection.

cards.heading: Free Access for New Players
cards.text: On August 31, 2007, Electronic Arts released Command & Conquer Gold as a free download for the series' twelfth anniversary. The package supplied disc images for both the GDI and Nod campaigns. Players could return to the 1995 strategy game or discover it for the first time through an official release from the series' publisher.

cards.heading: Compatibility and Active Maintenance
cards.text: Running C&C Gold on a newer PC could still require compatibility instructions. Operating systems, installers and display expectations had changed since the original release. The documentation accompanying the anniversary download addressed some of these differences. The game's return illustrated a practical part of maintaining older PC software: making the files available and helping players run them on current machines.

cards.heading: A Recognizable Strategy Grammar
cards.text: C&C Gold brought its two campaigns back to players with the resource gathering, base construction and specialised units of the original. GDI and Nod give the conflict different perspectives, supported by live-action sequences. Those videos also preserve the performance and production style of the CD-ROM era, alongside the interface and low-resolution battlefield.

main.title: Demo One
main.subtitle: A first tour of PlayStation on a single disc
main.summary: Bundled with the original European PlayStation, Demo One brought playable games, video previews and three-dimensional technology demonstrations together.

cards.heading: The disc inside the console box
cards.text: Demo One accompanied the European launch of PlayStation on 29 September 1995. The original disc, identified as SCES-00048, was packaged with the SCPH-1002 console. Its first printing used a folding cardboard sleeve with separate pockets for the disc and a registration card. It offered a way to explore several games without having to buy each one, turning the contents of the console box into a small introduction to its software library.

cards.heading: Games to try before buying
cards.text: The first edition included playable demonstrations of Wipeout, Loaded, Destruction Derby and Battle Arena Toshinden. A Total NBA '96 demonstration allowed the viewer to control its camera. Video previews presented further games, including Tekken, Ridge Racer and Warhawk. The distinction mattered: some entries invited the player to take control, while others simply showed a forthcoming game in motion. Later Demo One editions changed that selection.

cards.heading: The dinosaur, the manta and later editions
cards.text: Dino and Manta presented a dinosaur and a manta ray as three-dimensional technology demonstrations, alongside the V-CD material. These features made the disc more than a list of games to sample: it also showed the visual possibilities of the new machine. The Demo One name continued across several revisions bundled with later PlayStation consoles. The familiar title therefore described a changing collection, while the original 1995 edition remained a particular selection with its own menu, packaging and demonstrations.

main.title: Wipeout
main.subtitle: Anti-gravity racing meets club culture
main.summary: On September 29, 1995, WipEout accompanied the European launch of the original PlayStation.

cards.heading: A European PlayStation launch game
cards.text: WipEout accompanied PlayStation's European launch on September 29, 1995. Developed by Liverpool's Psygnosis, it sends anti-gravity craft through three-dimensional circuits. Electronic music, graphic design and British club culture shape its identity alongside the racing. Controlling a craft requires attention to inertia and a growing familiarity with each track, giving its futuristic presentation a demanding driving model.

cards.heading: A racing game with its own sound
cards.text: The project developed within Psygnosis around figures including Nick Burcombe and Jim Bowers. Electronic music was part of its conception as a racing experience, supplying energy and helping establish a recognisable style. Together with its art direction and graphics, the soundtrack connected WipEout to the club culture surrounding its 1995 audience.

cards.heading: Learning the air brakes
cards.text: A craft carries momentum into a corner. Air brakes help control its path, while contact with the track edges can cost valuable speed. Players must learn when to begin turning and how to prepare for the next section. Repeated laps make the circuit more familiar, allowing isolated corrections to become a smoother racing line.

cards.heading: Rivals can break the racing line
cards.text: Offensive tools let competitors interfere with one another. A well-timed attack can interrupt another craft's trajectory, while being hit can undo a carefully prepared corner. Players must watch their position among rivals as well as the road ahead. Even a familiar circuit can become less predictable when the other racers intervene.

main.title: Tactics Ogre
main.summary: Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together is a 1995 tactical role-playing game developed and published by Quest Corporation for the Super Famicom.

cards.text: Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together is a 1995 tactical role-playing game developed and published by Quest Corporation for the Super Famicom. It was later ported to the Sega Saturn (1996) and the PlayStation (1997), the latter released in North America in 1998 by Atlus USA. The second entry in the Ogre Battle series, the story takes place in the war-torn kingdom of Valeria, where protagonist Denim Powell works in a local resistance force against occupying powers, ending up caught in the ethnic conflicts driving the war. Battles are turn-based, taking place on grid-based maps from an overhead perspective with a focus on positioning and using character class abilities.

Production lasted two and a half years, with Ogre Battle creator Yasumi Matsuno acting as director, writer and lead designer. The storyline was inspired by conflicts in Europe and Asia, based heavily in personal and political drama over the fantasy-themed narrative of Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen. The gameplay, inspired by the video game Solstice, uses a chess-inspired combat system in contrast with the real-time battles of its predecessor. Hiroshi Minagawa was art director, while the characters were designed by Akihiko Yoshida. The music, composed by Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata, used the narrative as inspiration and remains fondly remembered by the composers.

The Super Famicom release sold 500,000 units in Japan and met with positive reviews. Later ports also met with strong sales and reviews, with many praising its gameplay and narrative. The PlayStation version was met with criticism for technical issues. It has since been remembered as one of the best in its genre. Matsuno left Quest Corporation after completing Tactics Ogre, joining Square (later Square Enix) and developing Final Fantasy Tactics (1997) and other titles set within its universe of Ivalice. Quest developed further titles in the series before being absorbed by Square in 2003. A remake of the same name for the PlayStation Portable was released in 2010.
